questions.stem: You are giving Samantha, 65, her biopsy result in general practice. After a warning shot you tell her in plain words that the biopsy shows cancer in the lower part of her food pipe. She goes quiet and looks down at her hands. What is the best thing to do next?
options: Explain the PET-CT and the treatment the team is likely to offer her
Pause, allow silence, then acknowledge how she is feeling
Reassure her that most oesophageal cancers are curable with surgery
Give her a written leaflet and book a follow-up visit to discuss it
questions.why: After the news is given, the next step is to stop talking, allow silence and respond to emotion (e.g. 'This is a lot to take in'). She cannot take in information until her emotional response has been acknowledged (SPIKES: Emotions before Strategy).
notes: Moving straight to the plan while she is in shock overloads her, and she will not take it in; strategy comes after acknowledging emotion.
This is false reassurance: staging is not complete, and oesophageal cancer often cannot be cured even when it is locoregional.
Ending the conversation as soon as she reacts leaves her alone with the news; she needs support and a plan now, with follow-up added on top.

questions.stem: At the results visit, Samantha, 65, still takes naproxen 500 mg twice daily for knee osteoarthritis. Bloods show Hb 112 g/L and ferritin 12 µg/L, and gastroscopy found an ulcerated, friable distal oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Her renal and liver tests are normal. What is the best change to her knee analgesia?
options: Continue naproxen and increase pantoprazole to 40 mg twice daily
Change naproxen to celecoxib 100 mg twice daily and continue pantoprazole
Stop naproxen; give regular paracetamol 1 g four times daily, liquid or dispersible
Stop naproxen; start regular oral oxycodone 5 mg four times daily
questions.why: NSAIDs add to bleeding from an ulcerated tumour and make iron deficiency worse, so stop naproxen. Regular paracetamol (max 4 g/day) is first-line for osteoarthritis, and a liquid or dispersible form is easier to swallow past a stricture.
notes: A higher PPI dose does not remove the antiplatelet and mucosal effects of naproxen on a friable, bleeding tumour.
COX-2 selective drugs still carry GI and cardiovascular risk and are not a good choice with active GI blood loss and an ulcerated cancer.
Regular opioids are not first-line for osteoarthritis, and they add constipation, sedation and falls risk; try paracetamol first.

questions.stem: Samantha, 65, has had reflux for 15 years. Her gastroscopy shows a C4M6 segment of salmon-coloured mucosa above the gastro-oesophageal junction, and biopsy shows intestinal metaplasia with high-grade dysplasia. Which cellular change defines Barrett's oesophagus?
options: Stratified squamous epithelium replaced by columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Columnar epithelium of the lower oesophagus replaced by stratified squamous cells
Basal cell hyperplasia and elongated papillae within intact squamous epithelium
Loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons in the lower oesophageal sphincter wall
questions.why: Repeated injury from acid and bile causes metaplasia: the normal stratified squamous lining is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells. This can progress through dysplasia to adenocarcinoma.
notes: This has the direction backwards: the normal oesophagus is squamous, and in Barrett's it becomes columnar.
These are the features of reflux oesophagitis in squamous mucosa, not metaplasia to a columnar lining.
This is the lesion in achalasia, a motility disorder; it is not a change in the epithelium.

questions.stem: While examining Samantha, 65, who has a suspected distal oesophageal cancer, you palpate the cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes. Enlargement of which node is classically linked to lymphatic spread from the stomach and gastro-oesophageal junction?
questions.why: Lymph from the abdomen and lower oesophagus drains through the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct, which empties at the left venous angle (where the left internal jugular and subclavian veins meet). Tumour spread along this route enlarges the left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node, also called Troisier's sign.
notes: The right supraclavicular nodes drain the right lung and mediastinum through the right lymphatic duct, not abdominal lymph through the thoracic duct.
The jugulodigastric node drains the tonsils and pharynx; it is not on the drainage path from the distal oesophagus or stomach.
Submandibular nodes drain the face, lips, tongue and floor of the mouth, not the gut below the diaphragm.
